cards.title: Direct-Response Ads: Brand-Regulated, Lifecycle-Dependent, Not a Foregone Choice
cards.summary: The source runs largely organic/affiliate-led ads and says DR intensity is a life-cycle choice — a brand can get away with lighter DR earlier; you may still need it later.
cards.use_when: Deciding how aggressively to run direct-response paid ads versus brand-led, organic and affiliate creative for your store.

cards.title: One Metric for Six Months: Sales
cards.summary: When asked to pick a single focus metric for the next six months, the source chose sales, saying 'sales cures all.'
cards.use_when: Choosing your store's north-star metric for a quarter or half-year, particularly in a growth phase when internal debate is diffuse.

cards.title: Enter Markets Too Small to Attract Competition
cards.summary: The source credits a lesson from an early investor: focus on markets and areas so small and overlooked that no one else is competing there.
cards.use_when: Choosing which niche, subcategory or customer segment to build your store around before broadening.

cards.title: Document the Journey From Day One
cards.summary: The source regrets not documenting their prior company's milestones and cites near-zero capital cost and high ROI of founder-led content and archives.
cards.use_when: Setting up content capture and archives for your store's early launches, partnerships and events.

cards.title: Choose Investors Who Have Operated, Not Just Allocated
cards.summary: Raise capital from operators who have built companies in your category rather than pure capital allocators who judge your brand on a spreadsheet.
cards.use_when: Deciding which investors to approach for a DTC or CPG brand raise, or evaluating an existing term sheet before signing.

cards.title: Manage Influencers With KPIs and Accountability
cards.summary: Treat influencers as third-party partners who need management, accountability and defined KPIs, not as a set-and-forget channel.
cards.use_when: Setting up or auditing an influencer and affiliate acquisition program for an ecommerce brand.

cards.title: Pick Mentors Who Have Scaled in Your Category
cards.summary: Prioritize advisors and mentors who have built and scaled in your specific category over generalist founders from unrelated sectors.
cards.use_when: Choosing advisors, board members or peer mentors while scaling a consumer brand into retail distribution.

cards.title: Treat Disciplined Content Creation as a Compounding Asset
cards.summary: Consistent, disciplined content production over a sustained period can turn a creator into a direct business driver and paid brand asset.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest in long-term content or creator partnerships as an acquisition and community channel for your store.

cards.title: Plan Retail Rollout by Channel, Not All at Once
cards.summary: Sequence retail distribution through specific chains on a staged calendar alongside your own DTC, feed and marketplace channels.
cards.use_when: Planning a retail distribution rollout for a consumer product and coordinating it with DTC and marketplace sales.

cards.title: Watch for Capital That Turns Your Business Into a Puzzle Piece
cards.summary: Institutional investors may reduce your brand to fit a spreadsheet, so know the trade-off before taking their money.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether to accept institutional capital versus staying smaller and founder-controlled for your ecommerce or CPG brand.

cards.title: The premium pricing triad: exclusivity, identity, storytelling
cards.summary: Three interlocking principles (exclusivity, identification, storytelling) let premium brands command far higher prices than commodity competitors.
cards.use_when: Positioning a store's brand and deciding the messaging angle for PDP copy, homepage narrative and landing pages before spending on acquisition.

cards.title: Research and psychology mapping to find what 'exclusive' means to your segment
cards.summary: Before writing premium copy, map each segment's psychological triggers so you know which exclusivity signals they actually value.
cards.use_when: Product selection and brand messaging decisions where you need to know which premium signals (craft, provenance, status, community) resonate with a specific customer segment.

cards.title: Define a marketing vector to keep sales messages on brand
cards.summary: A marketing vector sets the non-negotiable direction every ad must follow, so conversion-driven creative can be aggressive without diluting premium positioning.
cards.use_when: Planning acquisition creative and promotional campaigns when you need to balance conversion pressure against long-term brand equity.

cards.title: Premium ad format: 15-30 second lifestyle mini-documentaries
cards.summary: Premium brands replace static feature ads with short lifestyle mini-documentaries featuring real practitioners rather than models.
cards.use_when: Producing acquisition video creative for a premium or aspirational store where you need ads that sell without looking like discount spam.

cards.title: Measure premium creative on funnel and equity metrics, not ROAS alone
cards.summary: Evaluate premium ad creative using hook rate, video hold rate, CTR and cohort retention so early brand signals are visible before ROAS alone decides.
cards.use_when: Reviewing acquisition creative performance and deciding whether to keep or cut premium-style ad concepts that may not yet show direct return.

cards.title: Apply the three-step premium positioning process end to end
cards.summary: A repeatable three-step sequence: psychology mapping, defining the marketing vector, then optimizing for brand performance rather than revenue alone.
cards.use_when: Standing up or rebuilding a premium brand strategy across store narrative, ad creative and performance review.

cards.title: Define the brand as a promise and expectation shortcut
cards.summary: Reframe branding from logos and mass advertising to a specific promise that shortcuts customer expectations.
cards.use_when: Deciding what your store's brand actually stands for before running awareness campaigns or redesigning assets.

cards.title: Map positioning on an extreme emotional XY grid
cards.summary: Use unconventional emotional axes (not price vs features) to find a defensible positioning space.
cards.use_when: Choosing how to differentiate your store or product line in a crowded category.

cards.title: Use semiotics and vernacular to signal tribe belonging
cards.summary: Deliberate symbols, category vernacular, and visual cues attract the right tribe and filter out the wrong people.
cards.use_when: Designing PDP imagery, packaging, tone of voice, or ad creative that should signal who the product is for.

cards.title: Price as a status and value story
cards.summary: Use price architecture to communicate status, protect margin, and avoid the race to the bottom.
cards.use_when: Setting or restructuring pricing and tier architecture for products or bundles.

cards.title: Separate unmeasurable brand marketing from measurable direct marketing
cards.summary: Keep cultural brand engagement and ROI-tracked direct response in distinct buckets with distinct expectations.
cards.use_when: Allocating budget between brand-building campaigns and paid direct-response ads.

cards.title: Treat your email list as an owned permission asset
cards.summary: Earn consensual, anticipated communication with a tribe rather than renting attention from platforms.
cards.use_when: Building or managing email/SMS lifecycle communication and deciding what to send.

cards.title: Define the smallest viable market by worldview
cards.summary: Target a narrow psychographic cohort rather than a demographic mass market.
cards.use_when: Narrowing your target customer for product selection, messaging, and creative.

cards.title: Write the three-sentence marketing promise
cards.summary: Use the source's template to state audience worldview, desired outcome, and the promise of your product.
cards.use_when: Drafting or tightening a positioning statement for a store, product line, or landing page.

cards.title: Map status drivers: affiliation vs dominion
cards.summary: Identify whether your customers measure status by belonging (affiliation) or by winning and power (dominion).
cards.use_when: Choosing messaging, imagery, and bundle structure that appeals to your avatar's status motive.

cards.title: Discover objections and the internal narrative that blocks purchase
cards.summary: Surface the cognitive dissonance and fear of change behind a prospect's 'no' before optimizing the offer.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why qualified traffic fails to convert at cart or checkout.

cards.title: Match message to market sophistication: early adopters vs mass
cards.summary: Decide whether you are selling to neophiliacs craving the new or adapters who want safety, and adjust the pitch.
cards.use_when: Choosing creative angle, feature emphasis, and guarantee strength for a launch or campaign.

cards.title: Adopt a market-driven rather than marketing-driven orientation
cards.summary: Be market-driven by listening to and shaping the market's worldview, instead of marketing-driven and fixated on tactics, offers, and surface polish.
cards.use_when: When setting your store's product roadmap, brand positioning, or overall merchandising strategy and deciding what drives decisions.

cards.title: Find the lock before fashioning the key
cards.summary: Make products for customers you've identified rather than hunting for customers for products you already made.
cards.use_when: When choosing what to stock, design, or launch—product selection and range planning.

cards.title: Define the smallest viable market
cards.summary: Choose the minimum number of people you can delight and still make the effort worthwhile, then serve them obsessively.
cards.use_when: When deciding your target customer segment, niche, and initial launch audience instead of aiming at 'everyone'.

cards.title: Segment by worldview (psychographics), not demographics
cards.summary: Group customers by the stories they tell themselves and what they believe, not by looks, because worldview predicts how they'll respond.
cards.use_when: When defining buyer personas for merchandising, ad targeting, and PDP messaging.

cards.title: Run five steps of marketing in order
cards.summary: Sequence: invent something worth making with a story worth telling, build it for a few people, tell the matching story to the smallest market, spread the word, then show up for years.
cards.use_when: When planning a new product launch or brand-building campaign and deciding what to do first.

cards.title: Make a three-sentence marketing promise
cards.summary: Write and use a template promise stating who the product is for, who you'll focus on, and what engaging with it helps them get.
cards.use_when: When writing brand positioning, homepage copy, PDP headlines, or ad creative that must make a clear promise.

cards.title: Sell the feeling, not the feature
cards.summary: People don't want your product; they want what it will do for them and how it will make them feel—extend the drill-bit insight to the final emotion.
cards.use_when: When writing product descriptions, benefit-led landing pages, and ad creative for any SKU.

cards.title: Plan for the irrational, not the rational, customer
cards.summary: Assume people act on current irrational urges and cultural identity rather than weighing information and costs like a rational agent.
cards.use_when: When designing pricing, promotions, bundles, and checkout experiences that must account for real behavior.

cards.title: Set up market research trip like Penguin Magic
cards.summary: Build a specialist ecommerce experience with demonstration content, audience-specific insight, and customer reviews that cycle quality fast.
cards.use_when: When building a specialist store or category page and deciding what content and social proof to include.

cards.title: Use anticipation, personalization, and relevance to earn permission
cards.summary: Own a direct-contact permission asset—email—and earn the right to reach people without a middleman by making every message anticipated, personal, and relevant.
cards.use_when: When building and sending email lists, newsletters, and lifecycle campaigns; not for blast tactics.

cards.title: Create tension and relieve it at each step of the journey
cards.summary: Use tension deliberately—like the un-young-explained magic trick—and relieve it as customers progress toward their goal.
cards.use_when: When structuring PDP flow, upsells, content sequences, and onboarding to keep people moving.

cards.title: Design for loss aversion instead of the desire for gain
cards.summary: Frame the offer as keeping what they already have rather than shopping for something new, which can roughly double conversion in low-trust or low-income contexts.
cards.use_when: When structuring offers, trials, samples, or checkout for audiences that see buying as risk rather than fun.

cards.title: Choose a market-driven change and avoid two common stumbles
cards.summary: Define the specific change you're making happen, then avoid grandiosity and reverse-engineered buzzword change definitions.
cards.use_when: When writing your brand mission, category positioning, or campaign brief and deciding what change you're making.

cards.title: Use 'it's not for you' to filter and focus
cards.summary: Respectfully telling some people the product isn't for them sharpens your work for the people it is for—and protects your story from nonbelievers.
cards.use_when: When writing brand copy, choosing who to target in ads, and deciding how to handle critical reviews.

cards.title: Substitute 'students' for 'prospects and customers'
cards.summary: Reframe buyers as students you enroll and educate, shifting from a power dynamic of compliance to one of enrollment, choice, and care.
cards.use_when: When designing onboarding emails, content marketing, tutorials, and retention touchpoints.

cards.title: Apply the Open Heart Project's eight-part growth system
cards.summary: Build a community by starting from real empathy, serving the smallest viable market, matching worldview, making it easy to spread, keeping attention, offering depth, creating and relieving tension, and showing up often.
cards.use_when: When growing a subscription, membership, or community-driven store and deciding how to deepen customer relationships.

cards.title: Build a generous beacon, not a selfish USP
cards.summary: Find a spot on the map with edges that some people want, and signal it clearly, rather than maximizing market share with a narrow unique selling proposition.
cards.use_when: When defining your brand's differentiating position and best-for claim in a crowded category.

cards.title: Use storytelling, connection, and experience as core tools
cards.summary: Stories, connections, and experiences are timeless marketing tools that build trust and belonging more durably than any shiny digital shortcut.
cards.use_when: When planning content, community, and post-purchase experience instead of chasing new channel tactics.

cards.title: Recognize that marketing shifts from ads to empathy in a world of tiny whispers
cards.summary: The internet is the first mass medium not built for interruption, so effective marketing relies on empathy and service rather than buying attention.
cards.use_when: When allocating budget between paid interruption ads and building a brand that earns discovery, trust, and spread.

cards.title: Wait for better is not selling with a rational argument
cards.summary: Better is relative to what a specific person cares about, so frame your offer as better for those who share your market's values, not objectively superior.
cards.use_when: When crafting comparison claims, product superiority messaging, and promotional copy.

cards.title: Treat every purchase as a bargain the buyer thinks they're getting
cards.summary: People buy when they believe what they get is worth more than what they pay—so withholding options is a kind of theft from the buyer's narrative.
cards.use_when: When setting prices and constructing offers, and when writing nonprofit, donation, or premium pricing pages.

cards.title: Market to the human condition as Godin defines it
cards.summary: Everyone has a rich internal life, thinks they're right, is afraid and lonely and insecure, and cares about something—so empathy is the heart of marketing.
cards.use_when: When researching customer motivations, writing brand voice guidelines, and designing experiences for return customers.

cards.title: Position on a Two-Axis Map, Not on Competitors' Claims
cards.summary: Use a simple XY grid of customer-relevant attributes to find an uncrowded positioning quadrant for your store or product line.
cards.use_when: Choosing brand positioning, category angle, or PDP messaging when your store sells in a crowded category (snacks, supplements, apparel, tools) and you need a defensible reason to be chosen.

cards.title: Market to the Buyer, Not the End User
cards.summary: Dog food is bought by owners, not dogs — identify the person who actually makes the purchase decision and their emotional payoff.
cards.use_when: Product development, packaging or PDP copy for any store where the buyer differs from the user (pet products, kids' goods, gifts, B2B tools bought by a manager).

cards.title: Serve Early Adopters Differently From the Main Market
cards.summary: Neophiliacs want new, interesting and unfinished; the mainstream wants reliable and familiar — these need separate products, copy and channels.
cards.use_when: Deciding which SKUs or editions to launch first, how to sequence drops, and whether to write clever experimental copy or reassuring mainstream copy.

cards.title: Position as a Service: A Generous Signal Flare, Not a USP
cards.summary: Replace a self-serving unique selling proposition with a clear signal that helps the people looking for you find you.
cards.use_when: Writing your brand's core promise for the homepage hero, About page or ad hook when the current message is a generic superiority claim.

cards.title: Micro-Tribes: Sell Uniqueness and Belonging, Not Consensus
cards.summary: Outlier psychology shows people are drawn to small, distinct groups — a niche signal can beat a broadly appealing one.
cards.use_when: Community building, loyalty programs, or positioning a niche store or limited drop against a mass-market competitor.

cards.title: Run the 'It's a Test' Loop Instead of Betting on a Miracle
cards.summary: Shipping a real offer to real early adopters is faster and more honest than waiting for a hype-driven hit.
cards.use_when: Launching a new product, bundle or landing page when you're tempted to perfect it before exposing it to the market.

cards.title: Start From the Problem and the Change, Not the Product
cards.summary: Effective offers begin with a group to serve, a problem they want solved, and the change they want to make.
cards.use_when: Deciding what to build, stock or promote next; writing the top of a landing page; evaluating whether a new SKU has a real reason to exist.

cards.title: Sell the Emotional State, Not the Object
cards.summary: People buy feelings, status and connection; identify the feeling before designing the product.
cards.use_when: Writing PDP copy, choosing product photography or naming a new line, especially for non-essential goods.

cards.title: Find the Bear: Diagnose Non-Purchase as Fear
cards.summary: When customers don't behave as expected, look for fear blocking the purchase before blaming the offer's obvious features.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing low conversion, abandoned carts, low retention or poor response to a new offer.

cards.title: Design Remarkability Into the Product Itself
cards.summary: Products that work better when friends use them together grow by themselves; add-on marketing can't do that job.
cards.use_when: Designing referral mechanics, gifting options, multiplayer features, or shared/subscription plans in a store.

cards.title: Build Customer Traction in the Small Before Chasing Scale
cards.summary: Check daily usage, requests for improvement and peer insistence before believing a growth plan will work.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a new product line, store concept, or marketing budget increase — deciding whether to scale or fix the core first.

cards.title: Use the Thousand True Fans Sizing Rule for Niche Offers
cards.summary: A small number of superfans who buy nearly everything can sustain a business, so niche depth may beat mass reach.
cards.use_when: Sizing a niche subscription, membership or creator-style product line and deciding whether to chase a broad market instead.

cards.title: Scrapbook Proven Elements Instead of Inventing From Scratch
cards.summary: Improve conversion and design faster by breaking down trusted references into their parts and recombining them.
cards.use_when: Building a landing page, email campaign or new product listing when time is limited and you need a credible starting point.

cards.title: Price With the Ten-Times Question
cards.summary: Ask what would justify charging ten times more — the answer must be a different story and different scarcity, not more of the same.
cards.use_when: Pricing a premium tier, a luxury bundle, a membership, or a high-end physical product.

cards.title: Add an Offline or Human Element Online Retail Can't Copy
cards.summary: A physical or experiential differentiator lets a retailer compete with cheaper online sellers without a price war.
cards.use_when: Merchandising and positioning a physical store, showroom, pop-up, or local pickup experience against Amazon and other online retailers.

cards.title: Perform Emotional Labor Instead of Striving for Authenticity
cards.summary: In the marketplace, professional service and empathy beat raw authenticity; present the best version of the work, not every feeling.
cards.use_when: Customer service scripting, brand voice, founder-led content, UGC and support replies where the founder's mood and the brand's message conflict.

cards.title: Assert the Customer's Beliefs Before Choosing Channels
cards.summary: Research should surface what the audience believes and wants, then you assert a promise, not ask them to invent the product.
cards.use_when: Writing briefs for acquisition creative, ad hooks, or a pre-launch validation plan.

cards.title: Replace 'You Can Choose Anyone, and We're Anyone' with an Edge
cards.summary: Functional parity is table stakes; a true and generous edge is what makes a store the clear and obvious choice.
cards.use_when: Rewriting an undifferentiated homepage or category page that competes only on price.

cards.title: Start with the Smallest Viable Market, Not the Mass Market
cards.summary: Target a tiny audience who would genuinely miss you before trying to win the mass market.
cards.use_when: Choosing a positioning and target-customer focus for a new store, product line, or niche brand before spending on broad acquisition.

cards.title: Model the Grateful Dead's Small-Market Strategy for Repeat Buyers
cards.summary: The Dead concentrated everything on a tiny devoted audience rather than chasing radio hits—a template for super-fan-centric retail.
cards.use_when: Designing merchandising, drops, loyalty or community programs for a niche brand that wants high repeat purchase rather than broad one-time reach.

cards.title: Do Not Assume You Can Copy the Hit Machine Model
cards.summary: Hit-maker success exists but is rare; most brands succeed through connection and change rather than mass hits.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to pursue mass-market, hit-driven growth or a focused connection strategy for your store.

cards.title: Separate Criticism From Useful Advice You Can Act On
cards.summary: Critics describing their feelings are right but not useful; ask for advice framed around how to fit the person's worldview.
cards.use_when: Reviewing negative product reviews, customer feedback, or testing a new PDP/landing-page concept with real shoppers.

cards.title: Ask Why Non-Buyers Are Right (Empathy Exercise)
cards.summary: Complete the sentence explaining why people who did not buy made a rational choice given what they want and believe.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why an audience segment rejects your store, product or offer, or when repositioning after low conversion.

cards.title: Use the 'People Like Us Do Things Like This' Frame for Behavior Change
cards.summary: Decisions are driven by fitting one's cohort and status; normalize the new behavior inside the specific group you serve.
cards.use_when: Designing adoption campaigns, community programs or merchandising for a defined tribe (e.g., getting customers to try a new product category).

cards.title: Build an Exclusive Cohort, Not Just an Elite Brand
cards.summary: Exclusive (us vs them) organizations change culture and are controllable; elite status is external and fragile.
cards.use_when: Designing loyalty tiers, member communities, VIP programs or a brand identity based on insider belonging.

cards.title: Engineer Peer Pressure Through 'Cash for Status' Mechanics
cards.summary: Robin Hood Foundation's $101M night shows status trading, not the gala format, drives outsized giving.
cards.use_when: Designing high-value fundraising, charitable tie-ins, or VIP purchase experiences tied to social status.

cards.title: Plan for Pattern Match vs Pattern Interrupt
cards.summary: Fitting an existing buying pattern is easy; breaking one requires tension—target buyers whose patterns are not yet set.
cards.use_when: Deciding go-to-market approach for a new product category, new store, or a subscription that replaces an incumbent habit.

cards.title: Create Tension to Move Customers Forward (Not Fear)
cards.summary: Tension—the pull of being left behind or missing out—removes inertia; fear paralyzes instead.
cards.use_when: Writing acquisition or cart-recovery messaging for an offer that requires breaking an existing habit or decision.

cards.title: Decide Whether Your Store Is a Cab or an Agent of Change
cards.summary: Two paths: ride on demand as a replaceable cog, or create tension and then relieve it with your offer.
cards.use_when: Setting brand strategy and differentiating from commoditized competitors in your category.

cards.title: Remember the Status Quo Resists You Because of Status, Not Truth
cards.summary: The dominant narrative survives because of cultural status dynamics, not for lack of a better idea.
cards.use_when: Planning competitive entry against a market leader or legacy category belief.

cards.title: View Every Purchase Through Status Roles
cards.summary: Status is relative, perceived, learned, inertial, and shame can destabilize it—use it as a lens on purchase decisions.
cards.use_when: Designing product tiers, brand imagery, influencer partnerships, or loyalty perks where buyers signal who they are.
